segments.text: GURU CHAHAL: OK, this is an incredible group.
I was going to start, as you know, with a question around,
what's your definition of world model?
We will not do that because that's the next 20 minutes
of individual definitions.
Maybe if we have time at the end,
we'll come back to that for a set.
But I figured we'd just dig right in into some
of the meatier topics.
I listen to all of the chats today,
and I picked out a few where I figured
there might be some perhaps not disagreement, but slightly
different stances.
So I figured we'll just have a discussion.
This is not one of those-- here's the question,
let's go down--
I can't stand that, god.
So let's start with physics.
Anastasis, in your chat, your thesis
was, just by generating video, you
can generate an inside the model,
an inherent understanding of physics.
And you showed us some videos.
Why do you believe that?
And then, as you think through that,
I'd love for anyone else on the panel who's got a contrary
view to weigh in as well.
ANASTASIS GERMANIDIS: Yeah, so I think
that's mainly an empirical conclusion from just scaling
those models and measuring how well they
perform on different physics-related tasks.
In general, our approach has been
if you want to introduce inductive bias to make sure
that the model learns something well,
introduce those inductive biases in the data
that you're training on.
Don't introduce them in the architecture.
So we have very intentionally tried to learn everything
directly from pixels and not introduce any kind of 3D kind
of 3D based priors.
And we've seen that work pretty well.
Like at some level of scale, you get pretty good
geometric consistency.
That's something you can also measure quite well.
And so I don't think there is a fundamental reason in my mind
why that won't continue scaling.
GURU CHAHAL: Someone has to take the other side of this.
Is it true just generate video and you
get spatial knowledge inside suddenly a model
and becomes a world model?
JIM FAN: So I know that guru you said you don't want definitions
of world model.
Let me still have one and then I can ground the discussion.
So for my definition, it is a model
that predicts the next sensory state conditional actions.
Now, I think video is convenient.
In fact video is one of the sensors.
It's called an RGB camera.
But on a robotic system, you can have more than one RGB camera.
And, in fact, you have a lot more sensors.
And I will say there are many modalities missing
in today's discussion on world models in addition to videos.
There's tactile, there's force, are the invisibles that we also
need to put into these models to have a really
holistic simulation, holistic capture of how
the dynamics should evolve.
So I will say video is convenient.
Video is easy to scale.
It's already abundant, but that's not the full story.
GURU CHAHAL: OK, Sergey, you've done so many robots now
that are actually in deployment.
One of the few folks here who's closed the loop along with Jim
on exactly what's happening in real life.
What's your view?
SERGEY LEVINE: I guess what I would
say is that if you generate videos that people find
compelling, I think it's very easy to get into a situation
where you get a video that looks very good to people
but doesn't actually reflect a model's ability to simulate
the kind of counterfactual effects of physics
that you would care about.
So what that means is that when you give a model a prompt,
it doesn't have to produce a prediction about what
will happen to a real physical system in that situation
if it does something.
It just has to produce a result that
to you looks like a good reflection of that prompt, which
means that the model gets to choose.
And that choice is actually very, very important.
It gets to choose how to set everything up so that it
looks good to you.
Whereas if you need to actually plan and act in the real world,
you need to handle the actual situation
you're in, the actual plan that you're making,
and whatever kind of counterfactual effect
you might have.
So what this actually comes down to whether the model actually
understands physics or not, as Anastasis alluded to,
it has to do with the data, of course.
It's just that the data that we would
use to get really great videos is not the data that we
use to get counterfactuals.
If you train a model on really good driving data
and then you ask what happens if I drive into a building,
it will probably produce the building morphing
into a beautiful road, and you're
driving happily down the road.
And people have actually done this.
And that's exactly what happens.
So I think that the answer is like, yes, the model can handle
physics, but you have to be very careful not to let it fool you.
GURU CHAHAL: Right, right.
And while staying on this topic of what goes inside the model,
I'd love a little bit of debate on--
so we constantly hear or we're certainly hearing now--
and this I'll start with you, Jim, the era of VLAs is over
and the future is world action models.
Do you hold this view, Jim?
If so, why?
And then I'd love for more panelists to weigh in.
Is it VLA?
Is it WAM?
Is it both?
Or is VLA dead?
And it's all WAM going forward?
JIM FAN: Absolutely, yeah, I know
I talk a lot about World Action Models, WAMs, and VLAs.
I think it depends on the level of abstraction that we work on.
So there's the system 1 and system 2 thinking.
System 1 is fast and reactive motor skills.
System 2 is reasoning, like coding, tool calling,
all of that.
So I do think WAM is a very promising approach for system 1
because many of these physical common sense,
let's say, how do you grasp a cup?
It's very difficult to break down and describe every frame
through language tokens.
It's just quite difficult from a first principle point of view.
Now, regarding system 2, I would argue that OPUS
GPTs they are actually VLAs.
These models are agentic.
They take actions.
I would argue these are VLAs and, in fact,
more people use VLAs than they use WAM today because VLAs also
serve other purposes.
And that is the part where I'm discussing
my talk, agenetic scaling.
I think that's going to play a big part.
The VLAs, which are like the OPUS and the GPT of the world,
they're able to understand the world through some perception
and then calling tools and be able to help other research.
So I don't see maybe one completely replacing the other,
but it's really about the abstraction level
that you operate on top of.
GURU CHAHAL: Right.
Sergey.
SERGEY LEVINE: I actually think that it's slightly
the wrong question.
I mean, it's the right question for you to ask us,
but it's maybe slightly the wrong question for a researcher
to ask themselves because it puts
the model before the data in a way that maybe is not
actually quite right.
So the key to build a really good foundation model
is to be able to productively ingest
lots of very diverse data.
And video data is one of those data sources,
and it's a great data source.
Now, most VLAs that are actually good,
they are trained on video data, lots of video data.
It's just they're trained on it in a web scale pre-training
phase, which trains the understanding backbone.
So I actually don't think that the right answer is to say, oh,
is it VLA or is it video?
How do you use the most data?
And then on top of that, there's some kind of inductive bias.
But as Ilya Sutskever used to say,
"Inductive bias is training data in disguise."
So the effect of inductive bias might be large
when you're testing things at a small scale,
but it dissolves away once you scale things up.
So really, what we should do is say like,
OK, we're going to leverage as many data sources as possible
and then be pragmatic about what kind of outputs
the model has to leverage them.
GURU CHAHAL: Where you're--
sorry, Michael, go ahead.
MICHAEL SPRANGER: Yeah, maybe I can add two points
from our perspective.
So the first one is if you think about
the task that we are working on, like racing and table tennis,
I think language is actually not all that helpful.
It doesn't really-- you can describe how to do the skill,
but there's very little information.
I mean, there's in cognitive science,
there's this classic distinction between declarative and
procedural knowledge.
In order to ride a bike, you actually have to do it,
and you have to learn the physics of it.
The second one, I would say is if obviously vision I think
is a great thing to condition on.
At the same time, in some applications, you can't.
So for instance, if we are in game and we're shipping a game
to a customer and there's 20 agents racing,
we cannot render from 20 different viewpoints.
There's just not enough compute, let's say,
on PlayStation to do that, because most of the compute
goes into rendering for the customer like the player.
And so I don't think-- these are not yes/no questions.
They're sort of like, OK, what is the domain
that you're interested in?
What are you trying to solve?
What's the application downstream?
I will say that having large foundation models that
can capture visual knowledge and language model is in many cases,
really, really helpful.
But we also still need to distill the thing that we're
actually interested in a particular moment
and then maybe ship it to a consumer.
GURU CHAHAL: No, I like that answer.
It's not an either/or.
It really is use case dependent.
And both have really interesting applicability.
Wei--
ANASTASIS GERMANIDIS: Sorry, one more thing to add on.
The one versus VLA discussion is that generally, there's
a lot of convergence that's happening towards Omni
models that can actually predict both visual modalities,
OLA modalities, text modalities, and so
ultimately, it's to Sergei's point, it's all about,
what are you specializing in the model during pre-training on?
Are you specializing?
Is the data mixed bias towards more low level motion planning?
Is it biased towards high level reasoning?
So it's less about--
it's less about one more VLA architecture.
It's more about, what are you dedicating the capacity
of the model, ultimately?
And that tends to be the important factor.
GURU CHAHAL: Wei, backstage we were
talking about robots and simulated data
and stuff like that.
Today, from what you're seeing, how much of real robot skill
has to come from things like reinforcement
learning in the physical world versus the digital world?
And I'd love to then-- this is one
of those questions where I'm sure we all
have a point of view.
So I'd love to start with Wei and then maybe go down the line.
WEI ZHAN: Yeah, definitely.
So a great question.
So I want to separate that into different applications.
On one side, for autonomous driving,
so we care more about the behavior as well as
the visual modality.
And for those two, it's relatively easy for us
to scale that up from the real world data
and inject that into the synthetic world with a more
scalable way.
And for that part, right now it's more like this.
Many of the leading players for productionized end-to-end ADA
system is mainly focusing on utilizing the real world
data while some of the synthetic data
can be utilized for the post-training stage.
Well, we can see the trend that large scale synthetic
data can play the key role when more and more important
role for making the autonomy to be more robust and safe.
While on the robotic side, I think
what I learned at this very point
is that for tasks related to locomotion
for whole-body tracking, so the reinforcement
learning-based methods can be pretty useful
and even dominate that.
While for complex tasks like dexterous manipulation,
it could be a bit hard for us to either create
the high fidelity synthetic world capturing
many of the key physics attributes
or define the good reward function to really train
the corresponding policy in closed loop.
So at this very point, what I saw
is that behavioral cloning or imitation-based methods
are still dominating.
GURU CHAHAL: Let's fine-tune this question, Sergey,
as we come down to you a little bit more.
Let's say there are certain tasks you just
have to do in that robot's embodiment, extreme precision
in data collection versus simulation, egocentric data,
videos, et cetera.
What is that distribution?
How much of one do you need?
And how much of the other?
Are we still in the age where you just
need to do the task over and over again a million times?
Or can you do a vast majority of the work, either in-silico
or through egocentric data, et cetera?
What are you seeing in real-life now?
SERGEY LEVINE: Well, I think there's
two sides to that scale to the scales there.
There's the supply side and the demand side.
And this is where I think the future is
going to be very different from the present.
Because in the present, I would say that in robotics, we're
like in the bootstrap stage where we're
trying to figure out, what would it take to get models for robots
to be good enough so that they can actually be
used with end-to-end learning?
But we won't be in the bootstrap stage forever.
Eventually, we'll be in the stage
where there are as many robots deployed out there
as there are vehicles on the road today,
and there will be very plentiful sources
of data from robots interacting with the world autonomously.
And then reinforcement learning methods
that can use that real world data will
be tremendously important.
The other thing here is that the challenge, increasingly,
as the imitation learning methods that you mentioned
get better and better will actually be,
how do you bridge that last gap?
How do you go from a 98% successful robotic policy
to 100% successful policy?
And there the domain gap is really important
because you really want everything
to line up to be absolutely ideal.
So there I think we will also need reinforcement
learning in the real world.
But I think that that's what's coming in the future.
I don't think that's the state today.
I think your summary is an excellent summary of the state
today.
GURU CHAHAL: Yeah, Jim, I know you've done
some experimentation on this.
What are you seeing?
JIM FAN: Yeah, you know, Guru, I think great scientists invent,
greater scientists copy.
I absolutely love to copy homework from LLMs.
I look at them all the time.
So what do the LLM folks doing?
I think they are not just creating data anymore,
they're creating environments.
It's all about acquiring millions and millions of code
environments, and then doing RL in those environments
so that we can get the measles and the GPT source of today.
That's how they got here.
Not through imitation learning, eventually
through reinforcement learning.
So I see robotics to do something very similar,
that we need to build environments.
Then what are some options for environments?
Option number one is you run RL in the real world.
I think Sergey and PI has done exceptional work over there.
Absolutely important, the physics
is perfect because it's directing the real world.
And option number 2 is classical simulators
like Isaac Sim of the world.
But those simulators, the bottleneck
is not the simulation speed.
In fact, the simulation runs very, very fast.
But it's the assets, it's environments.
It's the tasks us that we used to need a lot of artists
to curate.
But now there are recipes called real to sim
that I believe is super promising to automatically scan
the world and transport the real world into a classical simulator
so you can both be data-driven while also relying
on classical fast physics solver.
So that's option number two.
And option three, back to world model,
I think one very practical use of video world model
is to use that as a neural simulator.
It's a data-driven program by data neural simulator.
Then it can take as input actions
and then generate videos and sensor states effectively
using it as environment.
But the thing is, it's going to run very slow,
but it will have a huge amount of diversity as much
as the world model can afford.
So ultimately, it's going to be reinforcement learning
across these three options for robotics
using different types of compute using different constraints.
So I would love to see this as a more holistic approach.
GURU CHAHAL: As we come up on time,
I'm going to ask two rapid fire questions that I love.
So first question, we'll start with you, Anastasis.
The most amazing demo in robotics or world models
you've seen recently, not from your company or team.
ANASTASIS GERMANIDIS: I've seen some great things internally.
But one demo or one model release I really like was by,
I believe, it's a new startup called Induction Labs.
The model is called Photon-1.
And it's effectively a world model
of based on screen recording, so a digital world model of sorts.
And they showed that you don't need
very often like when you're training computer use models
or you're post-training LLMs to do well in computer use
you're leveraging a lot of your text supervision
in addition to directly screen frames from UIs or screens.
But they train their model entirely
on essentially a video model on just screen recordings.
And they were able to show that they actually
get competitive performance with Gemini on computer use
or Gemini, one of the Gemini models with an order
of magnitude less compute.
So I found that pretty impressive.
GURU CHAHAL: I think that says more about the nature of work
we do on a screen than anything else.
Jim, something that made you go, wow.
JIM FAN: There's actually a robot that millions of people
already buy and use on a daily basis.
It's called Tesla FSD.
I've been driving Tesla since last year,
and honestly, I was amazed by the latest versions.
And it's like rush hours.
You can see the policy.
It's able to negotiate super well in super crowded lanes,
almost human like.
And I would say sometimes even better
than I would have driven myself.
So that gives you a lot of hope because that
is one physical system solving a very important task
autonomous driving.
And once you spin that physical data flywheel,
you get these huge performance gains, a quantum leap compared
to a couple of years ago.
So that's why in my talk today, I also
stressed the importance of having data collection fade
into the background.
The data collection cannot be intrusive.
And that's why when you have egocentric data on humans,
you are able to capture this dexterity without interfering
with what they're doing.
And that's the way that we can draw a parallel with FSD
and maybe someday get there for robotics.
And I would say that's something.
GURU CHAHAL: That's the example.
That's a great one.
Mika.
MICHAEL SPRANGER: So I'm going to pick something which is not
robotics itself but general intuition recently
released a world model really for Rocket League, which is
a game where cars play soccer.
It's kind of funny game.
What's amazing about that breakthrough, which
I think is about two weeks old or so,
was that this world model could render consistently
for different player views in that world.
So traditionally, world models are like,
it's me with the world, my actions in the world.
And that sort of unlocks sort of a multi-agent kind
of multiplayer, potentially interaction of multiple humans
in the world kind of future, which I think
is actually very important because we often
think in robotics purely about the task performance,
lifting a car, screwing something.
But the world is full of other agents.
It's full of things, of people or AIs
that we'll have to interact with.
And so I think this--
I didn't actually think was going to happen so soon,
I was thinking more like six to 12 months out
that this is going to happen.
But I think that's a major stepping stone
in the right direction.
GURU CHAHAL: That's a great example, Sergey,
SERGEY LEVINE: I have an example,
where there's kind of a moral to the story.
So a while back, there was this video
that went viral of the Boston Dynamics humanoid,
Atlas, doing a backflip.
And it kind of went viral because it
was around the same time where there
was a lot of-- this was around CES,
so there were a lot of demos of humanoids,
and people were making fun of this
because it does this backflip and it doesn't quite
stick the landing and it sort of freaks out and does
this really weird, unnatural motion, but then stays upright.
And people were saying like, oh, Boston Dynamics
is having all these problems.
Look at all the unitary robots doing these perfect backflips.
But the folks that work on robots looked at this
and they realized that actually, the Boston Dynamics
video is way more impressive because it actually
doesn't fall.
It freaks out.
Something really horrible happens, and it stays upright.
And then you remember, this is 170 kilogram robot.
It's way heavier, way more complex
than the more lightweight unitary robots.
And I think the lesson there is that, well, besides that Boston
Dynamics has great controls engineers
is that with robots, the demo is never quite what meets the eye.
The challenge is often not the things
that you see in the demo reel, it's
the degree of generalization, the ability of the system
to handle unfamiliar situations and failures
and also all the complexity behind it.
So it's often easy to be misled by the demo
and not realize what the really challenging problems there are.
GURU CHAHAL: Spoken truly like a person solving real world use
cases, I love it.
Wei.
WEI ZHAN: Yeah.
I would like to echo Jim for the Tesla
FSD, which is also taking over like most of my daily mileage.
And actually, there is an even more impressive thing
that I saw.
For that company I cannot disclose the name because I was
on the R&D car of that.
But that company can achieve similar kind
of level performance in super crowded kind of street
with a lot of pedestrians, cyclists, or other kind
of challenging situations for one hour
without any intervention from the driver side
while the onboard computer of that car
is only one seventh of the Tesla hardware
for compute and with even simpler kind of sensor
suite on the vehicle.
And for the robotic side, I think
one interesting thing I saw in the Acura and the CPR booth
this year is a Chinese startup called Sudo, which is also
trying to push the boundary for how
to utilize the synthetic data.
It's doing a lot of generalizable pick and place
tasks with relatively zero shot kind of thing.
Just let the audiences throw arbitrary things onto the table
and do that.
GURU CHAHAL: We're almost out of time.
I have to ask this one question.
The answer has to be a number, so we don't
have time for anything else.
A big movement in LLMs was what we called the cloud code moment.
And in the sense, that was the first use case
where commercial take off of these technologies happened.
In robotics, we think of the ChatGPT moment.
I want to define this next one after this, the cloud code
moment when the first commercial use case really takes off,
just rockets off.
And so your assessment will start this time with you,
Wei, your assessment of what year
does the first true commercially viable use case just
takes off in the wild.
And then if you have an idea for what that use case is,
just a word or two on the use case as well.
WEI ZHAN: Wow, that's pretty challenging.
I would just try my best to give the numbers.
So my guess would be around three years.
One thing is that--
we may also expect the data modality
to be somehow fulfilled, not just, for example,
a lot of egocentric or third person
view kind of large scale data, but also the necessary physics
modalities that can be well grounded and associated
with that.
So those kind of data accumulation
would take some time.
And that could be one of the gains
for having such kind of capability
for the robotic foundation model.
GURU CHAHAL: Perfect, three years.
Sergey.
SERGEY LEVINE: I promise I picked
this number before you answer, but my answer
is also three years.
I picked it in advance though.
So good shock.
But I actually don't know the area.
And I think that the key here is to have models
that are sufficiently general to radically lower
the barrier to exploring different applications
so that the community collectively
can get through as many different possibilities as
possible to arrive at that solution.
So I think the key there is a general model so we can
explore lots of applications.
GURU CHAHAL: That's a great point.
Three years, two three years.
Mika.
MICHAEL SPRANGER: I'm going to say three years to annoy.
GURU CHAHAL: Oh, come on.
MICHAEL SPRANGER: I'll say two.
And I think the area is going to be
somewhere in an industrial area because
of a semi-structured domain, possibly availability data.
It could be warehousing, could be manufacturing.
So I actually think that the technology is there.
It's more of a question of finding the right economics,
data inputs and environments where you can actually deploy,
which is where I think, for instance, deploying
large robots in the home in terms of safety issues
is probably further out.
So I think these semi-structured environments
where you can tailor the use case, bring in general models,
but also combine them with training on site or training
in simulation.
I think that's going to be a great.
GURU CHAHAL: Two years to the billion dollar moment.
Jim.
JIM FAN: Earliest, 2030.
And we'll have more robots than iPhones 2035.
And we're going to solve all robotics, everything,
personal robot, industrial robot, no later than 2040.
GURU CHAHAL: Amazing.
Anastasis, bring us home.
Are we going to go longer than four or less than two?
Those are the bounds right now.
ANASTASIS GERMANIDIS: I think there's a wide uncertainty
bar when it comes to deploying robotics for household tasks.
I think I agree with Michael in terms
of for very narrow enterprise use
cases in things like logistics or in the factory.
You're going to see deployment within the next two or three
years.
But when it comes to actually dealing
with the complexity of a home and being
able to operate autonomously at, like, many amounts
of reliability, it's going to I think probably a 5 to 10 years
seems more likely.
MICHAEL SPRANGER: Can I give an upper bound?
I think for some economies, and this is not
a technical argument, but we're going
to have to solve it in 10 years.
So if you take large Japanese corporations, for instance,
in manufacturing, any industry, 60% of the workforce
is 50 years or older.
And so in 10 years, they will all be gone.
GURU CHAHAL: So those are the bounds, 2 to 10.
MICHAEL SPRANGER: They'll have to solve it by then.
GURU CHAHAL: All right, all of you
are at the top of your domain top of your fields.
I really appreciate you spending your Saturday afternoon with us.
Thank you so much for the wonderful presentations
and the chat.
[APPLAUSE]
